This vignette follows a complete population-modelling workflow: define a
dynamic and statistical model, simulate a population, sample observations,
estimate the population parameters with nlmixr2, and inspect population and
individual predictions.

Physical quantities carry units throughout. Only the log-normal variability
`omega_CL` is dimensionless by definition. Solver and estimation backends work
on numerical scales internally, but compphysiol restores units at their public
boundaries.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(compphysiol)
library(units)
library(ggplot2)

has_nlmixr2 <- requireNamespace("nlmixr2est", quietly = TRUE)
```

## Dynamic model

We use a one-compartment model for an intravenous bolus. Drug amount is
measured in milligrams, central volume in litres, clearance in litres per hour,
and the observable concentration in milligrams per litre.

```{r}
#| label: dynamic-model
model <- compartment_model() |>
    add_compartment("Central", volume = 10 [L]) |>
    add_molecule(
        "drug",
        cmt = "Central",
        initial = 0 [mg],
        type = "amount"
    ) |>
    add_transport(
        from = "Central",
        to = NULL,
        molec = "drug",
        rate = "CL * c[drug, Central]"
    ) |>
    add_observable(C = c[drug, Central])

model
```

## Statistical model and true parameters

Individual clearances follow a log-normal distribution around the typical
clearance `CL_pop`. Concentration measurements have additive normal error. The
clearance median and residual standard deviation therefore carry their natural
physical units, whereas the standard deviation on the log-clearance scale is
dimensionless.

```{r}
#| label: statistical-model
statistics <- statistical_model(
    CL = lognormal(median = "CL_pop", sdlog = "omega_CL"),
    C = normal(sd = "sigma")
)

truth <- parameters(
    CL_pop = 1 [L/h],
    omega_CL = 0.25,
    sigma = 0.15 [mg/L]
)
```

## Simulate a population dataset

`sample_population()` realizes individual clearances with units. A common
unit-aware protocol supplies the dose and observation times;
`extend_protocol()` combines that protocol with every realized individual.

```{r}
#| label: population
set.seed(2026)

population <- sample_population(
    statistics,
    parameters = truth,
    n = 16,
    targets = "CL"
)

protocol <- experiment(
    dosing = dosing(
        time = 0 [h],
        amount = 100 [mg],
        molec = "drug",
        cmt = "Central"
    ),
    observations = observation_schedule(
        time = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24) [h],
        observable = "C"
    ),
    start = 0 [h]
)

simulation_studies <- extend_protocol(protocol, population)
```

The full collection is simulated in one call through rxode2. Each result is
then converted to long-format conditional predictions and sampled according to
the observation-level distribution. The sampled concentration values remain
in milligrams per litre.

```{r}
#| label: simulate-observations
#| eval: !expr has_nlmixr2
simulated <- simulate(
    model,
    experiment = simulation_studies,
    engine = rxode2_engine()
)

estimation_studies <- lapply(seq_along(simulation_studies), function(i) {
    observed <- simulated[[i]] |>
        as_observables_long() |>
        sample_observations(statistics, truth)

    experiment(
        dosing = simulation_studies[[i]]$dosing,
        observations = observed,
        start = simulation_studies[[i]]$start
    )
})
estimation_studies <- do.call(experiments, estimation_studies)

estimation_studies[[1]]
```

The individual clearances are used to generate the simulated predictions but
are deliberately not copied into `estimation_studies`: they are unknown random
effects in the estimation problem. The dose, time, and sampled concentration
data retain their units.

Before fitting, a spaghetti plot provides a quick view of the between-person
variation in the observed concentration-time profiles. Transient experiment
identifiers are added when the observation tables are combined for plotting;
the experiment collection itself remains unnamed.

```{r}
#| label: observed-spaghetti
#| eval: !expr has_nlmixr2
observed_data <- observations(estimation_studies)

ggplot(
    observed_data,
    aes(x = time, y = value, group = experiment, colour = experiment)
) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5) +
    labs(
        x = "Time",
        y = "Observed concentration",
        title = "Observed concentration-time profiles"
    ) +
    guides(colour = "none") +
    theme_minimal()
```

## Estimate with nlmixr2

The estimation problem contains unit-aware initial estimates for every
physical parameter. Log transformations enforce positivity in the numerical
optimizer without changing the scale on which estimates are reported.

```{r}
#| label: estimation
#| eval: !expr has_nlmixr2
specs <- c(
    CL_pop = parameter_spec(0.8 [L/h], transform = "log"),
    omega_CL = parameter_spec(0.2, transform = "log"),
    sigma = parameter_spec(0.2 [mg/L], transform = "log")
)

problem <- estimation_problem(
    model = model,
    experiments = estimation_studies,
    parameters = specs,
    statistics = statistics
)

fit <- estimate(
    problem,
    engine = nlmixr2_engine(
        control = list(print = 0L, maxOuterIterations = 100L)
    )
)

coef(fit)
standard_errors(fit)
fit$neg_log_lik
```

`coef()` and `standard_errors()` return parameter collections: clearance and
residual-error quantities retain their declared units, while `omega_CL`
remains dimensionless.

## Goodness-of-fit plots

For a mixed-effects fit, `PRED` is the prediction for the typical individual
and `IPRED` is conditional on each fitted individual's random effect. Selecting
the prediction type explicitly prevents these two meanings from being mixed.

```{r}
#| label: goodness-of-fit
#| eval: !expr has_nlmixr2
pred <- fitted(fit, "PRED")
ipred <- fitted(fit, "IPRED")

gof <- data.frame(
    OBS = observed_data$value,
    PRED = pred$value,
    IPRED = ipred$value
)

plot_limits <- range(c(gof$OBS, gof$PRED, gof$IPRED))

ggplot(gof, aes(x = PRED, y = OBS)) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#666666") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, colour = "#3366AA") +
    coord_equal(xlim = plot_limits, ylim = plot_limits) +
    labs(
        x = "Population prediction",
        y = "Observed concentration",
        title = "OBS versus PRED"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

ggplot(gof, aes(x = IPRED, y = OBS)) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#666666") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, colour = "#AA5533") +
    coord_equal(xlim = plot_limits, ylim = plot_limits) +
    labs(
        x = "Individual prediction",
        y = "Observed concentration",
        title = "OBS versus IPRED"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

The plotting table remains unit-aware because the observations and both kinds
of predictions already carry their concentration units. The axis labels derive
their units directly from these `units` columns.

## Individual concentration-time profiles

The individual predictions retain the experiment identifier and observation
times. This makes it possible to compare each fitted individual profile with
its observations without extracting information from the native nlmixr2 fit.
Here, solid lines connect the IPRED values at the sampling times, dashed lines
show PRED, and the observed values are shown as points. Prediction tables carry
the experiment identifier as a factor in experiment-collection order, so
facets appear in population order rather than lexicographic order.

```{r}
#| label: individual-profiles
#| eval: !expr has_nlmixr2
profile_data <- data.frame(
    individual = ipred$experiment,
    time = ipred$time,
    PRED = pred$value,
    IPRED = ipred$value,
    OBS = observed_data$value
)

ggplot(profile_data, aes(x = time, group = individual)) +
    geom_line(
        aes(y = PRED, linetype = "PRED"),
        linewidth = 0.7,
        colour = "#3366AA"
    ) +
    geom_line(
        aes(y = IPRED, linetype = "IPRED"),
        linewidth = 0.7,
        colour = "#3366AA"
    ) +
    geom_point(aes(y = OBS), size = 1.5, colour = "#AA5533") +
    facet_wrap(~ individual) +
    scale_linetype_manual(
        name = NULL,
        breaks = c("PRED", "IPRED"),
        values = c(PRED = "dashed", IPRED = "solid")
    ) +
    labs(
        x = "Time",
        y = "Concentration",
        title = "Individual predictions and observed concentrations"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

If nlmixr2 is not installed, the backend-dependent chunks are skipped while
the model and statistical specification remain visible.
